title: Practical Work
tagline: The 30-mark laboratory course: volumetric analysis, salt analysis, content-based experiments, project work and the class record.

overview.intro: Thirty of the hundred marks of CBSE Class XI Chemistry are awarded for practical work, distributed as Volumetric Analysis 8, Salt Analysis 8, Content Based Experiment 6, Project Work 4 and Class record and viva 4. This chapter teaches the course as it is actually examined: the laboratory techniques every student must handle, the purification and characterisation experiments, the pH and equilibrium investigations, the preparation of standard solutions and the titration arithmetic that underlies volumetric analysis, and the qualitative analysis scheme by which one anion and one cation are identified in a given salt. Because the practical examination is performed at the bench, the emphasis throughout is on what to do, what to observe and how to calculate.

learningOutcomes: Perform basic laboratory techniques safely, including cutting and bending glass tubing and boring a cork.
Determine melting and boiling points and carry out crystallisation to purify a solid.
Prepare standard solutions of oxalic acid and sodium carbonate and determine the strength of given acids and alkalis by titration.
Identify one anion and one cation in a given salt and detect nitrogen, sulphur and chlorine in an organic compound.

blocks.text: The first section of the practical course is manipulative. Glass tubing is cut by making a single firm scratch with a file across the tube and then pressing the thumbs apart on either side of the scratch, never sawing; the ends are smoothed in a bunsen flame. A tube is bent by heating a length of about 5 cm evenly in the flame and applying gentle pressure so that the bend forms gradually to the required angle, and a jet is drawn by heating a length and pulling the softened glass steadily apart. Corks are bored by rotating a cork borer at right angles to the cork, starting with the smaller bore, and the burr is removed from the borer after each turn. Every one of these operations is assessed in the practical examination for visually challenged students as identification of apparatus and of procedure, and for all students it is the difference between a working apparatus and a broken one.

Characterising a pure compound means measuring its melting point and boiling point, both of which are sharp for a pure substance and broad for an impure one. A melting point is determined by packing a small amount of the solid into a capillary tube, sealing the closed end, and heating it slowly in a Thiele tube or a melting point apparatus while stirring the oil; the temperature at which the first drop of liquid appears and the temperature at which the whole sample has liquefied are both recorded, and the range for a pure organic solid should not exceed 1-2 °C. Boiling point is determined by distillation of the liquid, recording the temperature at which a steady stream of vapour condenses at the delivery tube. Purification by crystallisation follows the standard sequence: dissolve the impure solid in the minimum hot solvent, filter hot if insoluble matter is present, cool slowly to let pure crystals form, filter the crystals, wash with a little cold solvent and dry.

learn.title: Experiments based on pH and on chemical equilibrium

blocks.text: The pH experiments build the acid-base theory into laboratory practice. The pH of solutions obtained from fruit juices, and of solutions of known and varied concentrations of acids, bases and salts, is found with pH paper or universal indicator: a strip is dipped, the colour is matched against the chart, and the value is read. Comparing the pH of strong and weak acids of the same concentration shows directly that a weak acid ionises only partially — 0.1 M HCl gives pH 1.0 while 0.1 M ethanoic acid gives about 2.9 — and the pH change in the titration of a strong base with acid, followed with a universal indicator, shows how steeply the hydrogen-ion concentration changes near the equivalence point. The common-ion experiment then takes a weak acid or weak base and adds a salt of the same ion: adding sodium ethanoate to ethanoic acid raises the pH, because the common ethanoate ions push the ionisation equilibrium backwards and suppress the release of hydrogen ions, which is exactly the buffer behaviour the theory describes.

The equilibrium experiment demonstrates Le Chatelier's principle with a visible colour change. In the ferric-thiocyanate system, Fe³⁺ (pale yellow) reacts with SCN⁻ to give the blood-red complex Fe(SCN)²⁺; adding more Fe³⁺ or more SCN⁻ makes the solution deeper red as the equilibrium shifts forwards, while dilution or the removal of one ion makes it paler as it shifts back. In the cobalt system the aqua complex [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink and the tetrachloro complex [CoCl₄]²⁻ is blue, so adding concentrated hydrochloric acid drives the equilibrium towards the blue chloro complex and adding water drives it back towards the pink aqua ion, with warming favouring the blue form because the forward change is endothermic. Both experiments give a reversible, repeatable colour response that students can relate directly to the position of equilibrium.

Volumetric analysis carries eight marks and rests on the preparation of standard solutions and the titration. A primary standard is a substance of high purity, stable in air, not hygroscopic and of known formula, and oxalic acid dihydrate and anhydrous sodium carbonate are the two used here. To prepare a standard solution of oxalic acid, accurately weigh the required mass of the pure crystals, transfer to a volumetric flask, dissolve in distilled water, make up to the mark and shake; the concentration in moles per litre is then known from the mass and the molar volume. A solution of sodium hydroxide, by contrast, cannot be weighed directly because it is hygroscopic and absorbs carbon dioxide, so it is standardised against the oxalic acid solution by titration.

The titration itself is performed by rinsing the burette with the solution it will hold, filling it, removing the air bubble below the tap, and recording the initial reading. Pipette a fixed volume of the other solution into a conical flask, add two or three drops of the appropriate indicator, and run the titrant in with constant swirling, slowing to dropwise addition as the end point approaches. The titre is the difference between the final and initial burette readings, and at least two concordant titres agreeing within 0.1 mL are averaged. The arithmetic then follows mole ratios: moles of standard = molarity × volume in litres; moles of the other reagent follow from the balanced equation, which is 1:1 for sodium hydroxide against oxalic acid and 1:2 for sodium hydroxide against carbonic acid; and the strength in grams per litre is molarity times molar mass. The same procedure with a standard sodium carbonate solution determines the strength of a given hydrochloric acid solution.

items.text: In a titration 20.0 mL of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide required 18.4 mL of oxalic acid. Find the molarity of the acid.
items.note: NaOH + H½H₂C₂O₄... the balanced equation is 2NaOH + H₂C₂O₄ → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O, so the mole ratio is 2:1. Moles of NaOH = 0.1 × 0.0200 = 0.00200, so moles of acid = 0.00100. Molarity of acid = 0.00100/0.0184 = 0.0543 M.

items.text: Calculate the strength of a sodium hydroxide solution if 20 mL of it required 19.5 mL of 1 M oxalic acid for complete neutralisation.
items.note: Moles of acid = 1 × 0.0195 = 0.0195. Since two moles of NaOH react with one mole of oxalic acid, moles of NaOH = 0.0390 in 20 mL, so in one litre the moles are 0.0390 × 50 = 1.95. Strength = molarity × molar mass = 1.95 × 40 = 78 g L⁻¹.

learn.title: Qualitative analysis and the detection of elements

blocks.text: Qualitative analysis carries eight marks and asks for one anion and one cation to be identified in a given salt. The anion is detected first, usually by the dilute acid test: the salt is treated with dilute sulphuric acid and the evolved gas is identified — carbon dioxide from carbonate turns lime water milky, sulphur dioxide from sulphite smells pungent and decolourises acidified potassium dichromate, hydrogen sulphide from sulphide blackens lead acetate paper, and nitrogen dioxide from nitrite is evolved with brown fumes. Where dilute acid gives no result the concentrated acid test is used, which liberates the halides: hydrogen chloride from chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate soluble in ammonium hydroxide, hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide behave similarly but with different colours and solubility, and sulphuric acid from sulphate gives a white precipitate with barium chloride that is soluble in hydrochloric acid. The cation is then detected by the hydrogen sulphide group separation in the presence of ammonium chloride and ammonium hydroxide, working through the groups until a characteristic precipitate appears, and every identification is confirmed by a second test before it is recorded.

The detection of nitrogen, sulphur and chlorine in an organic compound uses the sodium fusion test. A small sodium metal is heated in a fusion tube with a few drops of the compound until the tube is red hot, then plunged into distilled water; the covalently bound elements are converted into ionic sodium cyanide, sodium sulphide and sodium halide. Nitrogen is then detected by adding freshly prepared ferrous sulphate and heating, acidifying with dilute hydrochloric acid: a Prussian blue colour shows cyanide and hence nitrogen. Sulphur is detected by lead acetate solution, which gives a black precipitate of lead sulphide, or by sodium nitroprusside, which gives a violet colour. Halogen is detected by acidifying with nitric acid and adding silver nitrate: a white precipitate soluble in ammonium hydroxide indicates chlorine, a pale yellow precipitate indicates bromine and a yellow precipitate indicates iodine. Each of these tests is performed in the practical examination and recorded in the class record.

examFocus: The viva and class record test whether you understand your own experiment: know why each reagent was added, not only what happened.
Volumetric arithmetic is examinable in the theory paper as well as at the bench: standardisation, titre averaging and strength calculations are the highest-value practical skill.
Salt analysis marks depend on systematic work — preliminary test, group reagent, confirmatory test — rather than on guessing from colour alone.

questions.prompt: A pure organic solid typically shows a melting point range of:
questions.explanation: A pure compound melts sharply within about 1-2 °C because all molecules are held in the same crystal lattice. Even a few per cent of impurity disrupts the lattice, depressing the melting point and broadening the range, which is why the melting point is the standard test of purity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can be used directly as a primary standard?
questions.explanation: A primary standard must be pure, stable in air, not hygroscopic and of known composition. Oxalic acid dihydrate satisfies all of these. Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, hydrochloric acid is a gas in solution with an uncertain concentration, and ammonia solution loses ammonia — all three must be standardised against a primary standard instead.

questions.prompt: The gas that turns lime water milky when a salt is treated with dilute sulphuric acid is:
questions.explanation: Carbonate salts evolve carbon dioxide with dilute acid, and CO₂ precipitates calcium carbonate from lime water, making it milky; excess CO₂ redissolves the precipitate. Sulphur dioxide comes from sulphite and does not turn lime water milky in this way, hydrogen sulphide comes from sulphide and blackens lead acetate, and chloride would need concentrated sulphuric acid.

questions.prompt: In the titration of sodium hydroxide against oxalic acid using phenolphthalein, the end point is detected by:
options: the solution turning from pink to colourless
the solution turning from colourless to pink
the appearance of a white precipitate
questions.answer: the solution turning from pink to colourless
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in acid. The titration starts with sodium hydroxide in the flask, so the solution is pink, and as the acid is added the alkali is neutralised and the colour disappears at the end point; a permanent faint pink that persists for about 30 seconds is taken as the endpoint when titrating acid into alkali.

questions.prompt: The total marks allotted to the CBSE Class XI Chemistry practical examination are __________.
questions.explanation: The official evaluation scheme gives 30 marks: volumetric analysis 8, salt analysis 8, content based experiment 6, project work 4, and class record with viva 4. The remaining 70 marks are for the theory paper.

questions.prompt: The prussiate of soda test in qualitative analysis is used to confirm the presence of __________.
questions.explanation: Sodium nitroprusside (prussiate of soda) gives a violet colour with the sulphide ion produced by sodium fusion, confirming sulphur in the organic compound; lead acetate, giving a black precipitate of lead sulphide, is the alternative confirmatory test.

questions.prompt: Describe how a standard solution of oxalic acid is prepared and why sodium hydroxide cannot be prepared in the same way.
questions.answer: Oxalic acid dihydrate is a primary standard: it is weighed accurately on an analytical balance, transferred quantitatively into a volumetric flask, dissolved in distilled water and made up to the mark, so its concentration is calculated directly from the mass weighed and the volume of the flask. Sodium hydroxide cannot be prepared this way because it is deliquescent and absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air while being weighed, so the mass taken is not the mass of pure NaOH. It must therefore be prepared approximately and then standardised by titration against a standard oxalic acid solution of known concentration.
questions.explanation: The distinction rests on the defining properties of a primary standard — purity, stability and non-hygroscopic nature — and naming at least two of them earns the mark.

questions.prompt: Explain how the common-ion experiment with a weak acid and its salt demonstrates Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.answer: Take a solution of ethanoic acid, which is in equilibrium as CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺. Adding sodium ethanoate introduces acetate ions that are already on the product side of this equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts to oppose the change, consuming hydrogen ions as acetate combines with them to form more undissociated acid, so the hydrogen-ion concentration falls and the pH rises. The observation from the indicator or pH paper is therefore a higher pH for the mixture than for the weak acid alone, and it is the same shift that makes a buffer resist changes in pH when acid or base is added.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify which species was added, which side of the equilibrium it lies on, the direction of the shift, and the observed consequence, since all four are required for full marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the procedure for determining the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution by titrating it against a standard oxalic acid solution, and state how the titre is used to calculate the strength in grams per litre.
questions.answer: Prepare the standard oxalic acid solution first: weigh the required mass of pure oxalic acid dihydrate accurately, dissolve it in distilled water in a volumetric flask and make up to the mark, then calculate its molarity from molar mass 126 g mol⁻¹ for the dihydrate. Rinse the burette with the oxalic acid solution, fill it and remove the air bubble below the tap, then record the initial reading at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. Pipette 20.0 mL of the sodium hydroxide solution into a conical flask, add two or three drops of phenolphthalein, and run in the acid with constant swirling, slowing to dropwise addition as the pink colour begins to fade; the end point is the first drop after which the pink colour does not return within thirty seconds. Record the final reading; the titre is the difference, and at least two titres agreeing within 0.1 mL are averaged. Since oxalic acid and sodium hydroxide react in a 1:1 mole ratio in the standardised procedure... more precisely, two moles of NaOH react with one mole of oxalic acid, so moles of NaOH = 2 × molarity of acid × volume of acid in litres. Dividing by the volume of alkali used in litres gives the molarity of the NaOH, and multiplying by 40 g mol⁻¹ gives the strength in grams per litre. The burette and pipette readings must always be read at the bottom of the meniscus, and concordance of titres is the evidence that the value is reliable.
questions.explanation: The calculation chain is what carries the marks: titre to moles of standard, moles through the balanced ratio, moles to molarity of the unknown, and molarity to strength by the molar mass.

questions.prompt: A white salt gives a brisk effervescence with dilute sulphuric acid, and the gas turns lime water milky. On adding sodium hydroxide to the original salt solution a white precipitate appears that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide. Identify the anion and the cation, write the equations of the tests, and state which confirmatory test you would perform before recording the result.
questions.answer: The first observation identifies the anion. Effervescence with dilute acid together with a gas that turns lime water milky is the classic test for carbonate: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O, and CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ (milky) + H₂O, with the precipitate redissolving in excess carbon dioxide as soluble calcium bicarbonate. The second observation identifies the cation. Sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess, which means the hydroxide is amphoteric; among the listed cations this behaviour with cold sodium hydroxide points to zinc (or aluminium), giving Zn²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Zn(OH)₂ (white), followed by Zn(OH)₂ + 2OH⁻ → [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻ (soluble). Confirmatory tests must still be performed: for the anion, boil the salt with acid and pass the gas through lime water again, or show that the residue after heating gives an effervescence with acid; for the cation, add sodium hydroxide in excess to confirm the precipitate dissolves, then add ammonium chloride and hydrogen sulphide to precipitate zinc sulphide as a white precipitate insoluble in excess alkali. Only after both confirmations should the results be recorded in the record and reported to the examiner.
questions.explanation: The question rewards the disciplined order of salt analysis — preliminary test, group reagent, then confirmatory test — and penalises an identification recorded from a single observation, which is why a confirmatory test is explicitly requested.
